newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Montserrat volcano active, residents on higher alert.
newsitem.headline: Montserrat volcano active, residents on higher alert.

text.p: Authorities put residents on heightened alert on Monday as Montserrat's rumbling volcano spilled hot rock and ash over its southern flank and tossed an ash cloud 10,000 feet (3,000 metres) into the air.

The latest activity at the Soufriere Hills volcano coated the evacuated capital, Plymouth, with a thick layer of ash and forced authorities to reimpose a nighttime evacuation of the town of Richmond Hill, just to the north of Plymouth.
"For the first time we're getting significant pyroclastic flows down the south side of the mountain," said Angus Miller, a scientist at the Montserrat Volcano Observatory.

The pyroclastic flows -- fast-moving rivers of superheated rock and sulphurous gases -- reached about two miles (3 km) down the mountainside and altered the face of the landscape in the White River valley, damaging a couple of popular tourist spots, Miller said.
"The Great Alp waterfall is no longer a tourist attraction and the Galway's Soufriere hot spring, both have been covered by blocks of volcanic material," Miller said.

The activity came nearly a year after some 4,000 residents were evacuated from Plymouth and other towns at the south end of the British colony. The April 3 evacuation was the third since the Soufriere Hills volcano burst to life in July 1995 after nearly 400 years of virtual dormancy.

A portion of Galway's Wall at the volcano's peak collapsed as the volcanic material flowed out of the crater. Scientists said the mountain's ever-growing dome of volcanic material contained 64 million cubic yards (49 million cubic metres) of rock and ash and remained very dangerous.
"We're expecting further flows in the next few days," Miller said.
